The Five-Struct API

Describe a CT scan with five structs, simulate it, reconstruct it and read off its dose.

This notebook scans a Gammex 472 calibration phantom on a model of the GE Revolution Apex Elite twice, at 200 mA and at 50 mA, reconstructs both with filtered back-projection (FBP) and with Hybrid IR, and checks every number against physics: water at 0 HU, noise that scales with dose, and each calcium and iodine rod at its theoretical HU.

Every simulation in BasisSimulator.jl is specified by five plain Julia structs, one for each thing a CT scan needs, and run by three calls:

StructWhat It DescribesBuilt Here With
Phantomthe object: a labeled voxel mask, one XrayAttenuation.Material per label, the voxel sizecreate_gammex_472
EICTScanner / PCCTScannerthe hardware: geometry, detector, focal spot, filtration, bowtieREVOLUTION_APEX
CTProtocolthe acquisition: kVp, mA, views, rotation time, collimation, pitchCTProtocol(; ...)
SimOptionsthe physics: which effects the forward model includes, the noise seed, the projectorSimOptions(; ...)
ReconOptionsthe output grid: matrix size, in-plane field of view, z extentReconOptions(; ...)

Notebook Setup

The notebook activates the shared docs/ environment (which pulls BasisSimulator from this source tree) and loads CairoMakie for the figures.

import BasisSimulator as BS

Choosing the Device

BasisSimulator writes its kernels once, with AcceleratedKernels.jl, and runs them on whatever array type it is handed. GPUSelect.Storage() returns the array type of the GPU it finds (CuArray, MtlArray, ROCArray or oneArray), or Array when there is none. Moving the phantom mask to that type is the only thing that decides where the whole pipeline runs.

begin
    import GPUSelect
    # CuArray / MtlArray / ROCArray / oneArray, or Array on a CPU-only host
    AT = GPUSelect.Storage()
    to_gpu(x) = AT(x)
    GPU_BACKEND = (name = string(nameof(AT)),)
end;

Backend detected: CuArray

"""A blank drawing area at `position`: equal scales, no axes, limits `(x0, x1, y0, y1)`."""
function canvas(position, limits; background = COLORS.paper)
    ax = Mke.Axis(position; aspect = Mke.DataAspect(), backgroundcolor = background)
    Mke.hidedecorations!(ax)
    Mke.hidespines!(ax)
    Mke.limits!(ax, limits...)
    return ax
end;
"""The corners of a rectangle centred at `c`, `w` × `h`, its corners rounded by `r`."""
function rounded_rect(c, w, h, r)
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = c[1] - w / 2, c[2] - h / 2, c[1] + w / 2, c[2] + h / 2
    r = min(r, w / 2, h / 2)
    arc(cx, cy, θ0) = [
        Mke.Point2f(cx + r * cos(θ), cy + r * sin(θ))
        for θ in range(θ0, θ0 + π / 2; length = 8)
    ]
    return vcat(
        arc(x1 - r, y0 + r, -π / 2),
        arc(x1 - r, y1 - r, 0.0),
        arc(x0 + r, y1 - r, π / 2),
        arc(x0 + r, y0 + r, π),
    )
end;
"""A straight arrow from `a` to `b`; `head` is the arrowhead's size in pixels."""
function arrow!(
    ax,
    a,
    b;
    color = COLORS.muted,
    linewidth = 2.5,
    head = 15,
    linestyle = :solid,
)
    a, b = Mke.Point2f(a), Mke.Point2f(b)
    Mke.lines!(ax, [a, b]; color, linewidth, linestyle)
    t = b - a
    Mke.scatter!(
        ax,
        [b];
        marker = :utriangle,
        markersize = head,
        rotation = atan(t[2], t[1]) - π / 2,
        color,
        markerspace = :pixel,
    )
    return nothing
end;
"""
A box in a flow chart: centred at `c`, `w` × `h`, a bold `title` and an optional smaller
`subtitle`. `accent` colours its outline (and a strip down its left edge).
"""
function node!(
    ax,
    c,
    title;
    subtitle = "",
    w = 3.0,
    h = 1.0,
    accent = COLORS.violet,
    fill = COLORS.card,
    textcolor = COLORS.ink,
    subcolor = COLORS.muted,
    titlesize = 19,
    subtitlesize = 15,
    code = false,
)
    Mke.poly!(
        ax,
        rounded_rect(c, w, h, 0.14);
        color = fill,
        strokecolor = accent,
        strokewidth = 2,
    )
    strip = rounded_rect((c[1] - w / 2 + 0.06, c[2]), 0.12, h - 0.1, 0.05)
    Mke.poly!(ax, strip; color = accent)
    font = code ? "DejaVu Sans Mono Bold" : :bold
    dy = isempty(subtitle) ? 0.0 : 0.17 * h
    Mke.text!(
        ax,
        c[1] + 0.05,
        c[2] + dy;
        text = title,
        align = (:center, :center),
        fontsize = titlesize,
        font,
        color = textcolor,
    )
    isempty(subtitle) ||
        Mke.text!(
            ax,
            c[1] + 0.05,
            c[2] - 0.22 * h;
            text = subtitle,
            align = (:center, :center),
            fontsize = subtitlesize,
            color = subcolor,
        )
    return nothing
end;
"""
A flow chart: `nodes` maps a key to `(x, y, title, subtitle, accent)` (subtitle and accent
optional), `edges` lists `from => to` pairs, drawn as arrows between the boxes' edges, and
`labels` (optional) puts a note on an edge. Returns the canvas.
"""
function flow_chart!(position, nodes, edges; limits, w = 3.0, h = 1.0, labels = Dict())
    ax = canvas(position, limits)
    box(key) = nodes[key]
    function port(from, to)
        a, b = box(from), box(to)
        if abs(b[2] - a[2]) < 1.0e-6
            # side by side
            s = sign(b[1] - a[1])
            return (a[1] + s * w / 2, a[2]), (b[1] - s * w / 2, b[2])
        elseif abs(b[1] - a[1]) < 1.0e-6
            # one above the other
            s = sign(b[2] - a[2])
            return (a[1], a[2] + s * h / 2), (b[1], b[2] - s * h / 2)
        else
            # leave sideways, arrive on the facing side
            s = sign(b[1] - a[1])
            return (a[1] + s * w / 2, a[2]), (b[1] - s * w / 2, b[2])
        end
    end
    for (from, to) in edges
        p, q = port(from, to)
        if abs(p[1] - q[1]) < 1.0e-6 || abs(p[2] - q[2]) < 1.0e-6
            # straight across or straight down
            arrow!(ax, p, q)
        else
            # a right-angled connector: across to the gap's middle, along it, then in
            mx = (p[1] + q[1]) / 2
            Mke.lines!(
                ax,
                Mke.Point2f[p, (mx, p[2]), (mx, q[2])];
                color = COLORS.muted,
                linewidth = 2.5,
            )
            arrow!(ax, (mx, q[2]), q)
        end
        haskey(labels, from => to) &&
            Mke.text!(
                ax,
                (p[1] + q[1]) / 2,
                q[2] + 0.12;
                text = labels[from => to],
                align = (:center, :bottom),
                fontsize = 15,
                color = COLORS.muted,
            )
    end
    for (_, n) in nodes
        node!(
            ax,
            (n[1], n[2]),
            n[3];
            subtitle = length(n) >= 4 ? n[4] : "",
            accent = length(n) >= 5 ? n[5] : COLORS.violet,
            w,
            h,
        )
    end
    return ax
end;
"""
A CT gantry seen along z, centred at the origin: the source(s) at radius `sid` (one per entry
of `angles`, degrees), the fan, the detector arc at `sdd` from each source, and a round object
of radius `r_object`. Draws on `ax` in the colours of `dark` (the locator band) or paper.
"""
function gantry!(
    ax;
    sid = 5.4,
    sdd = 9.5,
    angles = (90.0,),
    fan_deg = 50.0,
    r_object = 2.0,
    detector_colors = (COLORS.cyan,),
    labels = ("Tube",),
    dark = true,
    object = true,
)
    ink = dark ? COLORS.night_ink : COLORS.ink
    ring = dark ? COLORS.night_card : COLORS.card
    Mke.poly!(ax, Mke.Circle(Mke.Point2f(0, 0), sid + 0.9); color = ring)
    Mke.poly!(
        ax,
        Mke.Circle(Mke.Point2f(0, 0), sid - 1.6);
        color = dark ? COLORS.night : COLORS.paper,
    )
    for (k, θ) in enumerate(angles)
        θ = deg2rad(θ)
        s = Mke.Point2f(sid * cos(θ), sid * sin(θ))
        half = deg2rad(fan_deg / 2)
        # the fan, from the focal spot to the detector arc (a circle about the source)
        edge = Mke.Point2f[
            s + sdd * Mke.Point2f(cos(θ + π + φ), sin(θ + π + φ))
            for φ in range(-half, half; length = 40)
        ]
        Mke.poly!(
            ax,
            Mke.Point2f.(vcat([s], edge));
            color = (COLORS.beam, 0.22),
            strokewidth = 0,
        )
        Mke.lines!(ax, edge; color = detector_colors[mod1(k, end)], linewidth = 9)
        Mke.scatter!(ax, [s]; marker = :rect, markersize = 26, color = ink)
        Mke.scatter!(ax, [s]; marker = :circle, markersize = 9, color = COLORS.beam)
        Mke.text!(
            ax,
            s * 1.18;
            text = labels[mod1(k, end)],
            align = (:center, :center),
            fontsize = 17,
            font = :bold,
            color = ink,
        )
    end
    object &&
        Mke.poly!(
            ax,
            Mke.Circle(Mke.Point2f(0, 0), r_object);
            color = (COLORS.blue, 0.55),
            strokecolor = ink,
            strokewidth = 1.5,
        )
    return ax
end;
"""
The dark locator band that opens a notebook: `n` panels side by side, each a canvas with
`limits`, its `titles[i]` and `subtitles[i]` underneath. Returns the figure and the canvases;
draw into them, then show the figure.
"""
function locator_band(titles, subtitles; limits, size = (1500, 560))
    fig = Mke.Figure(;
        size,
        backgroundcolor = COLORS.night,
        figure_padding = (10, 10, 18, 10),
    )
    axes = [
        canvas(fig[1, i], limits[i]; background = COLORS.night)
        for i in eachindex(titles)
    ]
    for i in eachindex(titles)
        Mke.Label(
            fig[2, i],
            titles[i];
            fontsize = 25,
            font = :bold,
            color = COLORS.night_ink,
            tellwidth = false,
        )
        Mke.Label(
            fig[3, i],
            subtitles[i];
            fontsize = 17,
            color = COLORS.night_muted,
            tellwidth = false,
        )
    end
    Mke.rowgap!(fig.layout, 1, 8)
    Mke.rowgap!(fig.layout, 2, 2)
    return fig, axes
end;
blend

c mixed toward base (the paper): t = 1 is c itself, t = 0 is base.

"""`c` mixed toward `base` (the paper): `t = 1` is `c` itself, `t = 0` is `base`."""
function blend(c, t; base = COLORS.paper)
    return Mke.RGBf(
        t * c.r + (1 - t) * base.r,
        t * c.g + (1 - t) * base.g,
        t * c.b + (1 - t) * base.b,
    )
end
gammex_insert

A Gammex 472 material's insert, (element, mg_per_mL), or nothing for water and air.

"""A Gammex 472 material's insert, `(element, mg_per_mL)`, or `nothing` for water and air."""
function gammex_insert(material)
    m = match(r"([\d.]+) mg/ml (Calcium|Iodine)", material.name)
    return m === nothing ? nothing : (element = m[2], mg_per_mL = parse(Float64, m[1]))
end
gammex_color

The colour a Gammex 472 material is drawn in: water blue, calcium red, iodine green, deeper for more.

"""The colour a Gammex 472 material is drawn in: water blue, calcium red, iodine green, deeper for more."""
function gammex_color(material; base = COLORS.paper)
    insert = gammex_insert(material)
    if insert === nothing
        return blend(COLORS.blue, 0.42; base)
    elseif insert.element == "Calcium"
        return blend(COLORS.red, 0.3 + 0.7 * insert.mg_per_mL / 600; base)
    else
        return blend(COLORS.green, 0.3 + 0.7 * insert.mg_per_mL / 20; base)
    end
end
draw_gammex!

A slice of Gammex 472 labels drawn on ax in its material colours, dx cm per pixel, centred on the isocentre (air left clear). annotate writes each rod's concentration (mg/mL) on it.

"""
A slice of Gammex 472 `labels` drawn on `ax` in its material colours, `dx` cm per pixel, centred
on the isocentre (air left clear). `annotate` writes each rod's concentration (mg/mL) on it.
"""
function draw_gammex!(ax, labels, materials, dx; annotate = true, fontsize = 14)
    n1, n2 = size(labels)
    clear = Mke.RGBAf(0, 0, 0, 0)
    colour(l) = startswith(materials[l + 1].name, "Air") ?
        clear :
        Mke.RGBAf(gammex_color(materials[l + 1]))
    lut = Dict(l => colour(l) for l in unique(labels))
    Mke.image!(
        ax,
        (-n1 / 2 * dx, n1 / 2 * dx),
        (-n2 / 2 * dx, n2 / 2 * dx),
        [lut[l] for l in labels];
        interpolate = false,
    )
    annotate || return ax

    for l in unique(labels)
        insert = gammex_insert(materials[l + 1])
        insert === nothing && continue
        pixels = findall(==(l), labels)
        x = (sum(p[1] for p in pixels) / length(pixels) - (n1 + 1) / 2) * dx
        y = (sum(p[2] for p in pixels) / length(pixels) - (n2 + 1) / 2) * dx
        deep = insert.element == "Calcium" ?
            insert.mg_per_mL >= 300 :
            insert.mg_per_mL >= 7.5
        value = insert.mg_per_mL >= 10 ? round(Int, insert.mg_per_mL) : insert.mg_per_mL
        Mke.text!(
            ax,
            x,
            y;
            text = string(value),
            align = (:center, :center),
            fontsize,
            font = :bold,
            color = deep ? Mke.RGBf(1, 1, 1) : COLORS.ink,
        )
    end
    return ax
end
dimension!

A dimension line from a to b, arrowheads at both ends, text beside its middle.

"""A dimension line from `a` to `b`, arrowheads at both ends, `text` beside its middle."""
function dimension!(
    ax,
    a,
    b,
    text;
    align = (:left, :center),
    offset = (10, 0),
    fontsize = 16,
)
    m = (Mke.Point2f(a) + Mke.Point2f(b)) / 2
    arrow!(ax, m, a; linewidth = 1.8, head = 11)
    arrow!(ax, m, b; linewidth = 1.8, head = 11)
    Mke.text!(ax, m; text, align, offset, fontsize, color = COLORS.ink)
    return nothing
end
callout!

A label at at with a thin leader line to the point to.

"""A label at `at` with a thin leader line to the point `to`."""
function callout!(
    ax,
    at,
    to,
    text;
    align = (:left, :center),
    fontsize = 16,
    color = COLORS.ink,
)
    Mke.lines!(ax, Mke.Point2f[to, at]; color = (COLORS.ink, 0.35), linewidth = 1.2)
    Mke.scatter!(ax, [Mke.Point2f(to)]; color = (COLORS.ink, 0.55), markersize = 7)
    Mke.text!(
        ax,
        at;
        text,
        align,
        fontsize,
        color,
        offset = (align[1] === :left ? 6 : -6, 0),
    )
    return nothing
end
draw_scanner!

scanner seen along z, to scale (one unit is 10 cm): the source, its fan, the detector arc, the scan field and a round object object_cm across, with the distances that define the geometry.

"""
`scanner` seen along z, to scale (one unit is 10 cm): the source, its fan, the detector arc, the
scan field and a round object `object_cm` across, with the distances that define the geometry.
"""
function draw_scanner!(ax, scanner; object_cm = 33.0)
    sid = scanner.source_to_isocenter / 100
    sdd = scanner.source_to_detector / 100
    fan = rad2deg(
        scanner.detector_cols * scanner.detector_col_size / scanner.source_to_isocenter,
    )
    gantry!(
        ax;
        sid,
        sdd,
        fan_deg = fan,
        r_object = object_cm / 20,
        labels = ("",),
        dark = false,
    )

    r_field = scanner.scan_diameter / 200
    Mke.lines!(
        ax,
        [
            Mke.Point2f(r_field * cos(t), r_field * sin(t))
            for t in range(0, 2π; length = 120)
        ];
        color = COLORS.violet,
        linestyle = :dash,
        linewidth = 2,
    )

    detector_y = sid - sdd
    mm(x) = isinteger(x) ? "$(Int(x)) mm" : "$(x) mm"
    guide(y, x; from = 0.0) = Mke.lines!(
        ax,
        Mke.Point2f[(from, y), (x, y)];
        color = (COLORS.ink, 0.25),
        linewidth = 1,
    )
    guide(sid, 8.6)
    guide(0.0, 8.6; from = object_cm / 20)
    guide(sid, -8.6)
    guide(detector_y, -8.6)
    dimension!(
        ax,
        (8.4, sid),
        (8.4, 0.0),
        "Source to Isocentre\n$(mm(scanner.source_to_isocenter))",
    )
    dimension!(
        ax,
        (-8.4, sid),
        (-8.4, detector_y),
        "Source to Detector\n$(mm(scanner.source_to_detector))";
        align = (:right, :center),
        offset = (-10, 0),
    )

    label(y, text, color; font = :bold) = Mke.text!(
        ax,
        0,
        y;
        text,
        align = (:center, :center),
        fontsize = 17,
        font,
        color,
    )
    label(sid + 0.62, "X-Ray Tube and Bowtie", COLORS.ink)
    label(sid - 1.25, "Fan $(round(fan; digits = 1))°", COLORS.ink; font = :regular)
    label(0.0, "Phantom\n$(round(Int, object_cm)) cm", COLORS.ink)
    label(
        -r_field - 0.45,
        "Scan Field, $(round(Int, scanner.scan_diameter / 10)) cm",
        COLORS.violet,
    )
    label(
        detector_y - 0.55,
        "Detector: $(scanner.detector_cols) Columns × $(scanner.detector_rows) Rows",
        COLORS.cyan,
    )
    return ax
end
draw_collimation!

scanner seen from the side, z across (stretched stretch×, units cm): the full cone of every detector row, the collimated beam of collimation_mm, the phantom object_z_cm long, and the rows_read rows the scan reads.

"""
`scanner` seen from the side, z across (stretched `stretch`×, units cm): the full cone of every
detector row, the collimated beam of `collimation_mm`, the phantom `object_z_cm` long, and the
`rows_read` rows the scan reads.
"""
function draw_collimation!(
    ax,
    scanner,
    collimation_mm,
    rows_read;
    stretch = 4.0,
    object_z_cm = 1.0,
)
    sid = scanner.source_to_isocenter / 10
    sdd = scanner.source_to_detector / 10
    magnification = sdd / sid
    detector_y = sid - sdd
    row_cm = scanner.detector_row_size / 10 * magnification * stretch
    half_detector = scanner.detector_rows * row_cm / 2
    half_beam = collimation_mm / 10 * magnification * stretch / 2
    half_read = rows_read * row_cm / 2
    half_object = object_z_cm * stretch / 2
    source = Mke.Point2f(0, sid)

    # the phantom, then the full cone (dashed) and the collimated beam
    Mke.poly!(
        ax,
        Mke.Rect2f(-half_object, -16.5, 2 * half_object, 33.0);
        color = (COLORS.blue, 0.45),
        strokecolor = COLORS.ink,
        strokewidth = 1,
    )
    Mke.poly!(
        ax,
        Mke.Point2f[source, (-half_detector, detector_y), (half_detector, detector_y)];
        color = (COLORS.beam, 0.08),
    )
    for s in (-1, 1)
        Mke.lines!(
            ax,
            Mke.Point2f[source, (s * half_detector, detector_y)];
            color = (COLORS.beam, 0.7),
            linestyle = :dash,
            linewidth = 1.5,
        )
    end
    Mke.poly!(
        ax,
        Mke.Point2f[source, (-half_beam, detector_y), (half_beam, detector_y)];
        color = (COLORS.beam, 0.7),
    )

    # the detector: every row, and the rows read in cyan
    Mke.poly!(
        ax,
        Mke.Rect2f(-half_detector, detector_y - 3.0, 2 * half_detector, 3.0);
        color = COLORS.card,
        strokecolor = COLORS.rule,
        strokewidth = 1,
    )
    Mke.poly!(
        ax,
        Mke.Rect2f(-half_read, detector_y - 3.0, 2 * half_read, 3.0);
        color = COLORS.cyan,
    )
    Mke.scatter!(ax, [source]; marker = :rect, markersize = 26, color = COLORS.ink)
    Mke.scatter!(ax, [source]; marker = :circle, markersize = 9, color = COLORS.beam)

    Mke.text!(
        ax,
        source + Mke.Point2f(0, 4);
        text = "X-Ray Tube",
        align = (:center, :bottom),
        fontsize = 17,
        font = :bold,
    )
    Mke.text!(
        ax,
        0,
        detector_y - 5;
        text = "$(rows_read) of $(scanner.detector_rows) Rows Read",
        align = (:center, :top),
        fontsize = 17,
        font = :bold,
        color = COLORS.cyan,
    )
    Mke.text!(
        ax,
        half_detector,
        detector_y - 5;
        text = "z →",
        align = (:right, :top),
        fontsize = 16,
        color = COLORS.muted,
    )
    full_mm = round(Int, scanner.detector_rows * scanner.detector_row_size)
    callout!(
        ax,
        (half_detector * 0.62, 22.0),
        (half_detector * 0.42, sid - (sid - detector_y) * 0.42),
        "Full Cone: $(scanner.detector_rows) × $(scanner.detector_row_size) mm\n= $(full_mm) mm at the Isocentre",
    )
    callout!(
        ax,
        (-half_detector * 0.5, 30.0),
        (0.0, 30.0),
        "This Scan's Beam:\n$(collimation_mm) mm at the Isocentre";
        align = (:right, :center),
    )
    callout!(
        ax,
        (-half_detector * 0.62, -8.0),
        (-half_object, -8.0),
        "Phantom, $(round(Int, 10 * object_z_cm)) mm Long";
        align = (:right, :center),
        color = COLORS.blue,
    )
    return ax
end
draw_view_arc!

One view of a turning gantry: the source's path (radius r), the arc Δθ_deg it turns through while the detector reads the view (drawn exaggeration× wider), and n sub-views, one at the middle of each 1/n of the arc.

"""
One view of a turning gantry: the source's path (radius `r`), the arc `Δθ_deg` it turns through
while the detector reads the view (drawn `exaggeration`× wider), and `n` sub-views, one at the
middle of each `1/n` of the arc.
"""
function draw_view_arc!(ax, n; Δθ_deg = 0.72, exaggeration = 28, r = 6.0)
    half = deg2rad(Δθ_deg * exaggeration / 2)
    arc(ρ, a, b) = [Mke.Point2f(ρ * cos(t), ρ * sin(t)) for t in range(a, b; length = 60)]
    Mke.lines!(ax, arc(r, π / 2 - 1.1, π / 2 + 1.1); color = COLORS.rule, linewidth = 3)
    Mke.poly!(
        ax,
        vcat([Mke.Point2f(0, 0)], arc(r + 0.6, π / 2 - half, π / 2 + half));
        color = (COLORS.violet, 0.1),
    )
    Mke.lines!(ax, arc(r, π / 2 - half, π / 2 + half); color = COLORS.violet, linewidth = 5)
    for s in (-1, 1)
        t = π / 2 + s * half
        Mke.lines!(
            ax,
            Mke.Point2f[(0, 0), ((r + 0.6) * cos(t), (r + 0.6) * sin(t))];
            color = (COLORS.violet, 0.5),
            linestyle = :dash,
            linewidth = 1.5,
        )
    end

    sources = [
        Mke.Point2f(r * cos(t), r * sin(t))
        for t in (π / 2 + half - (k - 0.5) * 2 * half / n for k in 1:n)
    ]
    for s in sources
        Mke.lines!(ax, [s, Mke.Point2f(0, 0)]; color = (COLORS.beam, 0.55), linewidth = 2)
    end
    Mke.scatter!(
        ax,
        sources;
        color = COLORS.beam,
        markersize = 18,
        strokecolor = COLORS.ink,
        strokewidth = 1.5,
    )
    Mke.poly!(
        ax,
        Mke.Circle(Mke.Point2f(0, 0), 1.65);
        color = (COLORS.blue, 0.5),
        strokecolor = COLORS.ink,
        strokewidth = 1.2,
    )
    Mke.text!(
        ax,
        0,
        r + 0.9;
        text = "One View, Δθ = $(Δθ_deg)°",
        align = (:center, :bottom),
        fontsize = 17,
        font = :bold,
        color = COLORS.violet,
    )
    return ax
end
source_at

Where BasisSimulator puts the source at gantry angle θ (radians), sid from the isocentre: view 1 starts below it.

"""Where BasisSimulator puts the source at gantry angle `θ` (radians), `sid` from the isocentre: view 1 starts below it."""
source_at(θ, sid) = Mke.Point2f(-sid * sin(θ), -sid * cos(θ))
column_through

The detector column (1-based, fractional) that the ray from the source at gantry angle θ through the point p (cm) reaches. Column numbers grow clockwise across the fan.

"""
The detector column (1-based, fractional) that the ray from the source at gantry angle `θ`
through the point `p` (cm) reaches. Column numbers grow clockwise across the fan.
"""
function column_through(p, θ, scanner)
    s = source_at(θ, scanner.source_to_isocenter / 10)
    central = -s
    ray = Mke.Point2f(p) - s
    γ = atan(
        central[1] * ray[2] - central[2] * ray[1],
        central[1] * ray[1] + central[2] * ray[2],
    )
    radians_per_column = scanner.detector_col_size / scanner.source_to_isocenter
    return (scanner.detector_cols + 1) / 2 -
        γ / radians_per_column +
        scanner.detector_col_offset
end
draw_view!

One view sketched to scale (cm): the Gammex slice labels, the source at gantry angle θ, its fan and detector arc, and the ray through the point p with the dexel it lands on.

"""
One view sketched to scale (cm): the Gammex slice `labels`, the source at gantry angle `θ`, its
fan and detector arc, and the ray through the point `p` with the dexel it lands on.
"""
function draw_view!(ax, θ, p, scanner, labels, materials, dx)
    sid = scanner.source_to_isocenter / 10
    sdd = scanner.source_to_detector / 10
    half = scanner.detector_cols *
        scanner.detector_col_size /
        scanner.source_to_isocenter /
        2
    s = source_at(θ, sid)
    toward = atan(-s[2], -s[1])
    arc = Mke.Point2f[
        s + sdd * Mke.Point2f(cos(toward + φ), sin(toward + φ))
        for φ in range(-half, half; length = 40)
    ]
    Mke.poly!(ax, vcat([s], arc); color = (COLORS.beam, 0.16))
    draw_gammex!(ax, labels, materials, dx; annotate = false)
    Mke.lines!(ax, arc; color = COLORS.cyan, linewidth = 7)

    d = Mke.Point2f(p) - s
    hit = Mke.Point2f(s + sdd * d / sqrt(d[1]^2 + d[2]^2))
    Mke.lines!(ax, [s, hit]; color = COLORS.red, linewidth = 2.5)
    Mke.scatter!(
        ax,
        [hit];
        color = COLORS.red,
        markersize = 13,
        strokecolor = COLORS.ink,
        strokewidth = 1,
    )
    Mke.scatter!(ax, [s]; marker = :rect, markersize = 20, color = COLORS.ink)
    Mke.scatter!(ax, [s]; marker = :circle, markersize = 7, color = COLORS.beam)
    return ax
end

1. The Phantom

A Phantom holds three things: a labeled mask (a 3-D array of unsigned integers, one region label per voxel), a material per label (an XrayAttenuation.Material, which gives the simulator μ(E) at every energy of the spectrum) and the voxel size (dx, dy, dz) in cm. It is centred on the isocentre unless you pass an origin.

create_gammex_472 builds the Gammex Model 472 multi-energy phantom: a 33 cm solid-water body with seven calcium rods (50–600 mg/mL) on an inner ring and seven iodine rods (2–20 mg/mL) on an outer ring, each 28 mm across.

phantom_cpu = BS.create_gammex_472(
    n_voxels = 512, # in-plane voxels across the 35 cm field
    n_slices = 16,  # axial slices
    fov_cm = 35.0,
    z_cm = 1.0,
);

The mask is UInt8 of size 512 × 512 × 16, with voxels of 0.684 × 0.684 × 0.625 mm and 27 entries in its material table (entry L + 1 is the material of label L; labels the phantom doesn't use are air). Phantom is parameterised on its mask's array type, so moving the mask to the device once is enough: every forward projection of this phantom then runs there.

phantom = BS.Phantom(
    to_gpu(phantom_cpu.mask),
    phantom_cpu.materials,
    phantom_cpu.voxel_size,
    phantom_cpu.origin,
    phantom_cpu.extent,
);

2. The Scanner

The scanner is the hardware: everything that stays the same from one scan to the next. There are two families, one per detector type, sharing a ScannerGeometry (source and detector distances, detector array, focal spot, gantry, flat filter, bowtie):

  • EICTScanner: an energy-integrating scintillator detector (material, depth, fill factors, detection gain, electronic noise);

  • PCCTScanner: a photon-counting detector (sensor, energy thresholds, dead time and pile-up, binning; its charge sharing and noise are its Geant4 response table's).

Each constructor rejects the other family's keywords, so a photon-counting parameter can't end up on a scintillator by accident. A clinical scanner is a documented constant: REVOLUTION_APEX models the GE Revolution Apex Elite (256 rows of 0.625 mm, 834 columns, a curved Gemstone detector, GE's large-body bowtie and a clinical DAS with 3500 e⁻ of electronic noise), and its docstring gives the source of every value. A variant copies every parameter and replaces the keywords given: EICTScanner(REVOLUTION_APEX; detector_rows = 64).

Hardware here, acquisition in the protocol

Anything that changes from scan to scan (kVp, mA, views, rotation time, collimation, pitch) belongs to CTProtocol. That split is what lets one scanner run a sweep of protocols, as the two scans below do. This scanner has 256 rows × 834 columns, a :arc detector and the :ge_revolution_large bowtie.

3. The Protocol

The acquisition. Two protocols share everything except the tube current: a standard-dose scan at 200 mA and a low-dose scan at 50 mA, both 120 kVp, 500 views in a 1 s rotation, 5 mm of collimation and 4.5 mm of extra aluminium filtration.

protocol_standard = BS.CTProtocol(
    kVp = 120,
    mA = 200.0,
    views = 500,
    rotation_time = 1.0,
    collimation_mm = 5.0,               # nominal beam width N·T
    additional_filters = [("Al", 4.5)], # on top of the scanner's 2.5 mm flat filter
);
protocol_lowdose = BS.CTProtocol(
    kVp = 120,
    mA = 50.0, # a quarter of the dose
    views = 500,
    rotation_time = 1.0,
    collimation_mm = 5.0,
    additional_filters = [("Al", 4.5)],
);

The detector is 256 × 0.625 mm = 160 mm wide at the isocentre; collimation_mm = 5.0 lights only its central rows. The simulator adds symmetric guard rows where the cone beam needs them to cover the whole reconstruction cylinder at the edge of the field. Leave collimation_mm unset to use the full detector; add pitch and n_rotations for a helical scan (notebook 11).

4. The Physics

SimOptions chooses the effects of the forward model. Every effect is on by default except optical crosstalk: fill factor, energy-dependent detector efficiency, patient scatter, focal-spot blur, quantum and electronic noise, detector lag and the anode heel effect. The polychromatic spectrum, the bowtie and beam hardening are always part of the model. Turn an effect off to measure its contribution. projector = :dd_fast (the default) is the anti-aliased distance-driven projector that walks the volume once for the whole spectrum; :siddon, the point-sampled ray tracer, is kept for comparison.

The detector integrates while the gantry turns. A clinical detector reads each view for the whole view period, while the gantry sweeps Δθ = 360° / views, so each reading is the intensity averaged over that arc: the object blurs along the rotation, more the farther it sits from the isocentre, while the noise, counted once per view, stays independent from view to view. view_samples samples the arc at sub-views (the midpoint rule, in intensity, before scatter, noise and the detector effects). Every clinical scanner in these notebooks uses view_samples = 5, which costs five forward projections per view.

sim_opts = BS.SimOptions(
    # fixed noise realisation: same seed + same inputs = same sinogram
    seed = 1234,
    projector = :dd_fast,
    # the detector integrates over the arc of each view (5 sub-views)
    view_samples = 5,
    # Switch individual effects off, e.g.:
    # use_scatter     = false,   # no patient scatter
    # use_heel_effect = false,
    # use_focal_spot  = false,
    # use_noise       = false,   # the noiseless expected sinogram
);

Detector-specific physics lives on the scanner

SimOptions carries only the effects both detector families share. Patient scatter is the scanner's Geant4 scatter kernels (BasisMonteCarlo's library, scatter_kernels), superposed on the phantom's own rays; every clinical constant names its kernels (a download of about 250 MB per scanner, cached after the first scan; BS.scatter_kernels(entry; path) reads a local copy), and a scanner the library has no entry for (scatter_kernels = "") throws unless use_scatter = false. The detector then subtracts the scatter it estimates from its own data, as a real one does (scatter_correction = true on both families). Pile-up and the count-noise blend are fields of PCCTScanner; the scintillator's fill factor, energy response, optical crosstalk and lag (use_fill_factor, use_detector_efficiency, detector_efficiency_mode, use_optical_crosstalk, use_lag) are fields of EICTScanner, e.g. EICTScanner(BS.REVOLUTION_APEX; use_lag = false).

5. The Image Grid

ReconOptions is the output grid: matrix size, in-plane field of view and z extent, centred on the isocentre. Here the 5 mm beam is reconstructed as eight 0.625 mm slices on a 512 × 512 grid over 35 cm (0.68 mm pixels). The algorithm and its filter are chosen where they are used, when the reconstruction workspace is created.

recon_opts = let
    slice_thickness_mm = 0.625
    n_slices = round(Int, protocol_standard.collimation_mm / slice_thickness_mm)
    BS.ReconOptions(
        matrix_size = (512, 512, n_slices),
        fov_cm = 35.0,
        z_cm = protocol_standard.collimation_mm / 10,
    )
end;

6. Simulate

create_workspace does all the set-up once: it builds the scan geometry, resolves the source spectrum through the filters and bowtie, and allocates every device buffer on the phantom's backend. simulate! then runs the forward model into ws.sinogram, the log-transformed line integrals -log(I/I₀) of size (columns, rows, views), noise included. The same constructor serves both detector families: for a PCCTScanner it builds the photon-counting workspace, and simulate! returns one sinogram per energy bin.

simulate! also returns the dose of the acquisition. The CTDI follows IEC 60601-2-44: the simulated beam is transported by Monte Carlo through the 32 cm PMMA body phantom, and the air kerma is integrated over a 100 mm pencil chamber at the centre and at the periphery, so it follows this scanner's spectrum, filtration and bowtie rather than a lookup table. Each scan runs inside a let block that keeps only CPU copies, so the device buffers are released before the next scan starts.

sim_std = let
    ws = BS.create_workspace(scanner, protocol_standard, sim_opts, recon_opts, phantom)
    result = BS.simulate!(ws, phantom, protocol_standard, sim_opts)

    out = (sino = Array(ws.sinogram), geom = ws.geom, dose = result.dose)
    ws = nothing
    GC.gc(true) # hand the device memory back now
    out
end;
DoseReport (body32, 120 kVp, 200.0 mAs/rotation, axial, increment 5.0 mm) CTDIvol = 13.72 mGy DLP = 6.86 mGy·cm over 0.5 cm CTDIw = 6.861 mGy/100 mAs (centre 4.151, periphery 8.217; ±0.48 % statistical) free-in-air kerma at isocentre = 16.16 mGy/100 mAs N·T = 5.0 mm, beam 5.0 mm, filters [("aluminum", 2.5), ("Al", 4.5)], bowtie :ge_revolution_large
sim_std.dose

Reading the Sinogram

Each view is one gantry angle; each detector column is one ray of the fan. A sinogram stacks the views side by side, so a rod off the isocentre swings across the columns as the gantry turns and traces a sine. The sketches follow the ray through the 600 mg/mL calcium rod at four views; the red dots on the sinogram are the columns it reaches.

The Low-Dose Scan

The same two calls with protocol_lowdose. The phantom, scanner, physics and grid are reused unchanged, which is the point of keeping them in separate structs.

sim_low = let
    ws = BS.create_workspace(scanner, protocol_lowdose, sim_opts, recon_opts, phantom)
    result = BS.simulate!(ws, phantom, protocol_lowdose, sim_opts)

    out = (sino = Array(ws.sinogram), geom = ws.geom, dose = result.dose)
    ws = nothing
    GC.gc(true)
    out
end;
DoseReport (body32, 120 kVp, 50.0 mAs/rotation, axial, increment 5.0 mm) CTDIvol = 3.43 mGy DLP = 1.72 mGy·cm over 0.5 cm CTDIw = 6.861 mGy/100 mAs (centre 4.151, periphery 8.217; ±0.48 % statistical) free-in-air kerma at isocentre = 16.16 mGy/100 mAs N·T = 5.0 mm, beam 5.0 mm, filters [("aluminum", 2.5), ("Al", 4.5)], bowtie :ge_revolution_large

The beam is identical, so CTDIvol scales with the tube current alone: the low-dose scan delivers 0.25 of the standard dose. CTDIw of this beam is 6.86 mGy per 100 mAs. The Monte Carlo's statistical uncertainty is ±0.48 %. Pass dose_kwargs = (; phantom = :head16) to simulate! for the 16 cm head phantom.

Repeated Noise Draws

Everything before the noise (the view-integrated forward projection and the physics that precedes the noise, scatter included) is the same for every noise draw of one phantom, protocol and workspace. simulate!(...; keep_projection = true) returns it as result.projection, and simulate!(...; projection) draws a new realisation from it, with the seed of the SimOptions it is given, without projecting again. A noise study over many seeds, or a noise-free reference (use_noise = false) that shares the noisy scan's projection, pays for the projection once.

noise_draws = let
    ws = BS.create_workspace(scanner, protocol_standard, sim_opts, recon_opts, phantom)
    # one full simulation that keeps everything before the noise …
    t_full = @elapsed (
        kept = BS.simulate!(
            ws,
            phantom,
            protocol_standard,
            sim_opts;
            report_dose = false,
            keep_projection = true,
        )
    )
    # … and a second noise realization drawn from it with another seed
    opts_2 = BS.SimOptions(;
        seed = 5678,
        projector = sim_opts.projector,
        view_samples = sim_opts.view_samples,
    )
    BS.simulate!(
        ws,
        phantom,
        protocol_standard,
        opts_2;
        report_dose = false,
        projection = kept.projection,
    )
    sino_reused = Array(ws.sinogram)
    # the same seed simulated from scratch, for comparison
    BS.simulate!(ws, phantom, protocol_standard, opts_2; report_dose = false)
    identical = Array(ws.sinogram) == sino_reused
    t_reuse = @elapsed BS.simulate!(
        ws,
        phantom,
        protocol_standard,
        opts_2;
        report_dose = false,
        projection = kept.projection,
    )
    ws = nothing
    kept = nothing
    GC.gc(true)
    (t_full = t_full, t_reuse = t_reuse, identical = identical)
end;

A full simulation of the standard scan took 0.51 s; a noise draw from its kept projection took 0.11 s, 4.5× less. The draw from the projection is bit-identical to simulating the same seed from scratch.

7. Reconstruct

The Water Beam-Hardening Correction

The simulated sinogram is polychromatic: the spectrum hardens as it crosses the patient, so the line integrals grow more slowly than the path length, and an uncorrected reconstruction reads low in the middle of the body (cupping). calibrate_bhc_water removes that for water. For every detector column it resolves the full detected spectrum (tube, filters, bowtie, heel effect and detector efficiency: exactly the factors sim_opts switched on) and fits the polynomial that maps polychromatic water line integrals to monochromatic ones at the spectrum's mean energy. It has no tunable parameters, and nothing in it is fitted to the data being corrected; apply_bhc_water applies it to a sinogram. The reference energy and water μ that come with it are what to_hounsfield needs to put water at 0 HU. Both protocols share a beam, so one calibration serves both.

bhc = BS.calibrate_bhc_water(sim_opts, protocol_standard; scanner, geom = sim_std.geom);

Water BHC: 834 per-column polynomials · reference energy 74.7 keV · water μ = 0.18816 cm⁻¹

FBP and Hybrid IR Through One reconstruct!

reconstruct! dispatches on the reconstruction workspace, so the two algorithms differ only in the workspace you create. create_fdk_recon_workspace is filtered back-projection (Feldkamp–Davis–Kress for an axial scan, weighted FBP for a helical one) with the :standard kernel by default. create_hir_recon_workspace(...; strength) is Hybrid IR: an FBP start followed by ordered-subsets penalised weighted least squares with an edge-preserving Huber prior. strength is a percentage in steps of 10, read like the vendor dials (GE ASIR-V, Siemens SAFIRE): 0 is plain FBP, 60 the standard clinical setting. HIR's system matrix uses the same projector as the simulation (projector = sim_opts.projector), so it inverts the operator that made the data.

The function below is that whole chain and returns a CPU volume in HU.

"""
    reconstruct_hu(sim, bhc; algorithm = :fbp, strength = 60) -> Array{Float32, 3}

Water BHC, then FBP (`algorithm = :fbp`) or Hybrid IR (`algorithm = :hir`), then HU.
"""
function reconstruct_hu(sim, bhc; algorithm::Symbol = :fbp, strength::Integer = 60)
    sino = BS.apply_bhc_water(to_gpu(sim.sino), bhc)
    ws = if algorithm === :fbp
        BS.create_fdk_recon_workspace(sino, sim.geom, recon_opts.matrix_size)
    elseif algorithm === :hir
        BS.create_hir_recon_workspace(
            sino,
            sim.geom,
            recon_opts.matrix_size;
            strength,
            projector = sim_opts.projector,
        )
    else
        throw(ArgumentError("algorithm must be :fbp or :hir"))
    end
    μ = BS.reconstruct!(ws, sino, sim.geom)
    hu = Float32.(BS.to_hounsfield(Array(μ); μ_water = bhc.μ_water_ref))
    ws = nothing
    sino = nothing
    μ = nothing
    GC.gc(true)
    return hu
end;
hu_fbp_std = reconstruct_hu(sim_std, bhc; algorithm = :fbp);
hu_hir_std = reconstruct_hu(sim_std, bhc; algorithm = :hir, strength = 60);
hu_fbp_low = reconstruct_hu(sim_low, bhc; algorithm = :fbp);
hu_hir_low = reconstruct_hu(sim_low, bhc; algorithm = :hir, strength = 60);

8. Results

Where Each Number Is Measured

Noise is only meaningful inside one material. The phantom labels are carried onto the reconstruction grid with resample_to_recon, and the solid-water label is eroded by 3 pixels so that only pixels surrounded by water remain: the rods and their partial-volume edges are excluded. Each rod is measured in its own label eroded by 2 pixels. All statistics use the central slice; the edge slices of a cone-beam reconstruction see fewer complete rays.

water_roi = let
    labels = BS.resample_to_recon(
        phantom_cpu,
        sim_std.geom,
        recon_opts.matrix_size;
        method = :nearest,
    )
    nx, ny, nz = size(labels)
    kmid = (nz + 1) ÷ 2
    water = UInt8(BS.REGION_SOLID_WATER)
    r = 3 # erosion radius, voxels
    m = falses(nx, ny)
    for j in (1 + r):(ny - r), i in (1 + r):(nx - r)
        m[i, j] = all(labels[i + di, j + dj, kmid] == water for dj in -r:r, di in -r:r)
    end
    (labels = labels, kmid = kmid, mask = m)
end;
noise = let
    k, m = water_roi.kmid, water_roi.mask
    stat(v) = (mean = Float64(mean(v[:, :, k][m])), σ = Float64(std(v[:, :, k][m])))
    (
        fbp_std = stat(hu_fbp_std),
        hir_std = stat(hu_hir_std),
        fbp_low = stat(hu_fbp_low),
        hir_low = stat(hu_hir_low),
    )
end;

FBP vs Hybrid IR at Two Doses

The four reconstructions share physics, geometry and grid. Down the columns, only the tube current changes; across the rows, only the reconstruction. Quartering the dose should double the FBP noise (noise ∝ 1/√mAs) and leave every mean HU where it was. Hybrid IR at strength 60 should lower the noise at both doses without moving the means.

Water, central slice, 151452 pixels deep inside the solid-water body:

FBP noise ratio, 50 mA / 200 mA = 2.1×. Quantum noise alone predicts 2×; the fixed electronic noise of the detector weighs more at low dose and pushes the ratio a little above that. The package's calibration band for HIR at strength 60 is 25–35 % noise reduction.

Dose and Noise at Other Tube Currents

The two scans anchor a simple rule: CTDIvol is proportional to mAs (same beam, same phantom), and quantum-limited FBP noise scales as 1/√mAs. The table applies it to this protocol at other tube currents. The detector's electronic noise makes the real noise somewhat higher than this at low mA, as the measured 50 mA scan shows.

4

9. Verification

Pass/fail against physics-derived expectations. The theory for each rod is its monoenergetic HU at the BHC reference energy, computed from the same XrayAttenuation data that drove the simulation. The tolerance is max(15 HU, 15 %): a water-only BHC maps water exactly, but a dense calcium or iodine rod hardens the beam beyond the water curve. That residual grows with density (down to -8.9 % for calcium and -10.7 % for iodine, below), and a single-energy scan cannot resolve it; quantitative high-Z imaging is what the dual-energy and photon-counting VMI notebooks (03, 04) are for. Each rod must also read the same at both doses and in both reconstructions.

# Every rod's mean HU (central slice, its label eroded by 2 pixels) beside its theoretical HU
rods = let
    labels, k = water_roi.labels, water_roi.kmid
    refE, μw = bhc.reference_energy_keV, bhc.μ_water_ref
    nx, ny, _ = size(labels)

    # in-plane-eroded mask of one label on the central slice
    function eroded(lab; r = 1)
        m = falses(nx, ny)
        for j in (1 + r):(ny - r), i in (1 + r):(nx - r)
            m[i, j] = all(labels[i + di, j + dj, k] == lab for dj in -r:r, di in -r:r)
        end
        return m
    end
    slc(v) = @view v[:, :, k]

    out = NamedTuple[]
    for lab in 1:(length(phantom_cpu.materials) - 1)
        # material entry L + 1 is label L
        lab == Int(BS.REGION_SOLID_WATER) && continue
        m = eroded(UInt8(lab); r = 2)
        count(m) < 20 && continue
        mat = phantom_cpu.materials[lab + 1]
        theory = 1000 * (BS.compute_μ_at_energy(mat, refE) - μw) / μw
        fbp = mean(slc(hu_fbp_std)[m])
        hir = mean(slc(hu_hir_std)[m])
        fbp_low = mean(slc(hu_fbp_low)[m])
        tol = max(15.0, 0.15 * abs(theory))
        ok = abs(fbp - theory) <= tol &&
            abs(fbp - fbp_low) <= max(10.0, 0.03 * abs(theory)) &&
            abs(hir - fbp) <= max(10.0, 0.03 * abs(theory))
        push!(
            out,
            (
                material = mat,
                insert = gammex_insert(mat),
                theory = theory,
                fbp = fbp,
                hir = hir,
                fbp_low = fbp_low,
                tol = tol,
                ok = ok,
            ),
        )
    end
    out
end;

  • Five structs describe a scan. Phantom (the object), EICTScanner / PCCTScanner (the hardware), CTProtocol (the acquisition), SimOptions (the physics, including the view integration of a turning gantry) and ReconOptions (the output grid). Changing the dose meant changing one CTProtocol and nothing else.

  • Three calls produce an image. create_workspace sets everything up once, simulate! runs the forward model and reports the dose, and reconstruct! runs FBP or Hybrid IR, depending on the workspace it is given. Hybrid IR lowered the 200 mA water noise by 36.3 %; quartering the dose raised the FBP noise 2.1×.

  • A noise draw can reuse the projection, 4.5× faster than a full simulation and bit-identical to it.

  • Every scan reports its dose, from a Monte Carlo of the simulated beam in the IEC body phantom.

  • The standard reconstruction chain is calibrate_bhc_water → apply_bhc_water → reconstruct! → to_hounsfield; measure_radial_cupping is a QA measurement, not a correction. 14 of 14 rods sit within their tolerance of theory, and 8 of 8 checks pass.

  • Where it runs is decided by the phantom mask's array type (here CuArray); the same notebook runs on CUDA, Metal, ROCm, oneAPI or the CPU.

Every other notebook reuses this pattern: build the structs, create a workspace, simulate!, reconstruct!.
